macbethPage.title: Macbeth — Scene-by-Scene Analysis
macbethPage.intro: Grade 9 archive: Macbeth from the 2025–26 materials. Use it to practise analysis; the 9–13 November mock texts are not yet confirmed.
macbethPage.notice: These questions and themes come directly from your G9 English revision booklet.

themes.title: Major themes to track
items: Ambition — Macbeth's tragic flaw. 'Vaulting ambition which o'erleaps itself.'
Fate vs free will — are the witches showing the future or causing it?
Appearance vs reality — 'Fair is foul, foul is fair'; 'Look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under't.'
Guilt — blood as motif; Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking ('Out, damned spot').
Power — corrupting, isolating; tyranny vs rightful kingship.
Gender — Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here'; performative masculinity.
Supernatural — witches, ghosts, hallucinations as both real and psychological.
Order vs chaos — regicide breaks the Great Chain of Being; nature reflects political disorder.

act1.title: Act I — Temptation and decision
scenes: Scene 1 (Witches' opening): How does the chant set the tone? How does 'fair is foul' introduce themes? What does this short scene suggest about supernatural influence?
Scene 2 (Battle report): What qualities of Macbeth come through in the Captain's description? How does violent imagery shape early impressions? What might his celebrated violence foreshadow?
Scene 3 (Witches meet Macbeth): How does Macbeth react to the prophecy? Contrast Banquo's caution with Macbeth's curiosity. How does this scene introduce temptation?
Scene 4 (Duncan names Malcolm heir): Why is Macbeth's aside about 'black and deep desires' significant? How does it contrast appearance and reality?
Scene 5 (Lady Macbeth's soliloquy): What does she reveal about her ambitions and values? How does Shakespeare challenge traditional gender roles? Is she more ruthless than Macbeth here?
Scene 6 (Duncan arrives): Why is Duncan's description of the castle ironic? How does this scene explore deception?

Scene 7 (Macbeth's soliloquy and Lady Macbeth's persuasion): What reasons does Macbeth give for not killing Duncan? How does Lady Macbeth manipulate him? How responsible is Macbeth for his own choice?

act2.title: Act II — The murder
scenes: Scene 1 (Dagger soliloquy): What does the vision suggest about Macbeth's mental state? How does hallucination imagery create tension?
Scene 2 (After the murder): How do Macbeth's and Lady Macbeth's reactions differ? What is revealed through the blood and guilt motif?
Scene 3 (Porter scene + discovery): How does the Porter's comedy ironically heighten horror? How does Shakespeare suggest chaos now governs Scotland?
Scene 4 (Unnatural events): What do strange events in nature reflect about human affairs? How is divine order vs human ambition developed?

act3.title: Act III — Corruption of power
scenes: Scene 1 (Banquo's suspicion; murder planned): What suspicions does Banquo voice? How does power corrupt Macbeth here?
Scene 2 (Macbeths grow apart): How has their dynamic shifted? Could Macbeth now be more ruthless than Lady Macbeth?
Scene 3 (Murder of Banquo): Why is Fleance's escape symbolically important?
Scene 4 (Banquet and Banquo's ghost): What does Macbeth's reaction reveal about his guilt? How does the banquet mirror political disintegration?
Scene 5 (Hecate's plan): How does this scene develop ideas of fate, free will, and illusion?
Scene 6 (Lennox discusses unrest): How is tyranny contrasted with rightful kingship?

act4.title: Act IV — False security
scenes: Scene 1 (Apparitions): How does Shakespeare use equivocation? How is false security central to Macbeth's tragedy?
Scene 2 (Murder of Lady Macduff): How does focusing on innocence and family affect the audience?
Scene 3 (Malcolm and Macduff plan rebellion): Why does Malcolm test Macduff? How is rightful leadership constructed?

act5.title: Act V — Downfall
scenes: Scene 1 (Lady Macbeth sleepwalking): What does her unconscious speech reveal? How is the blood/washing motif used? Madness as justice or tragedy?
Scene 2 (Scottish forces gather): How is Macbeth's isolation suggested before battle?
Scene 3 (Macbeth clings to prophecies): How does denial and bravado show in his language?
Scene 4 (Birnam Wood marches): How is dramatic irony used? Is fate working with or against human agency?
Scene 5 ('Tomorrow' soliloquy): How does this reflect existential despair? Could Macbeth be sympathetic in his final moments?
Scene 6–8 (Final battle and death): How does Macbeth face death? Could his final fight partially redeem him?

keyQuotes.title: Key quotes (memorise these)
items: 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' (1.1, Witches) — establishes theme of appearance vs reality.
'I dare do all that may become a man; / Who dares do more is none' (1.7, Macbeth) — conscience speaking before he's overruled.
'Look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't' (1.5, Lady Macbeth) — deception advice.
'Is this a dagger which I see before me' (2.1, Macbeth) — hallucination before murder.
'Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?' (2.2, Macbeth) — overwhelming guilt.
'We have scorched the snake, not killed it' (3.2, Macbeth) — fear that threats remain.
'Out, damned spot! Out, I say!' (5.1, Lady Macbeth) — guilt manifesting in sleepwalking.
'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, / Creeps in this petty pace from day to day' (5.5, Macbeth) — nihilistic despair.

examFormatPage.title: Grade 9 archive — Q1a–Q1e practice
examFormatPage.intro: Historical Grade 9 practice: comparing written text and video. This is not a confirmed blueprint for the 9–13 November mocks or a future IB exam; follow current teacher instructions.

structure.title: Question structure
items: Q1a — describe or identify something simple (2 marks). Just give the fact.
Q1b — explain meaning of a phrase / device (3 marks). Use 'because' + technique name.
Q1c — comment on how a technique is created (2 marks). One technique + one effect.
Q1d — analyse the effect of a specific phrase (3 marks). Quote + technique + connotation + effect.
Q1e — compare and contrast both texts (20 marks). Full essay. Criterion A (Analysis) /10 + Criterion B (Organising) /10.

q1eStructure.title: How to structure Q1e — the comparison essay
q1eStructure.body: One possible plan: introduce both texts and your comparative claim; organise body paragraphs around shared ideas, using precise evidence from both; explain similarities and differences in method and meaning; conclude with what the comparison reveals. This is a practice scaffold. Use the actual task’s length, time and assessment instructions.

markScheme.title: Practice self-review descriptions
items: Strong analysis explains how precise details support a developed interpretation and comparison.
Developing analysis identifies relevant similarities and differences but may need fuller explanation.
General analysis summarises content or names techniques without showing their significance.
Clear organisation helps the comparison develop logically, with transitions between related points.
These are study descriptions, not an official IB mark scheme or a guaranteed band.

selfCheck.title: Self-check prompts
items: Did I quote from BOTH texts?
Did I name techniques (metaphor, lighting, sound, structure) accurately?
Did I explain the EFFECT of each technique, not just spot it?
Did I compare in every paragraph (not text-by-text)?
Did I write under timed conditions to build exam stamina?

progressTestPage.title: Progress Test — Vocabulary & SPaG
progressTestPage.intro: From the Progress Test Revision Booklet. Vocabulary banks for analytical writing, SPaG rules, British vs American spelling.

survivalVocab.title: Survival / cold setting vocabulary
survivalVocab.body: Glacial — extremely cold or related to glaciers; Inhospitable — difficult to live in, or unwelcoming; Barren — producing little vegetation; Crystalline — made of crystals or clear and sparkling; Desolate — deserted, bleak or deeply unhappy; Relentless — continuing without easing; Fragile — easily damaged; Endure — bear hardship or continue to exist; Eerie — strangely unsettling; Bleak — exposed and unwelcoming, or without hope; Solitude — the state of being alone; Resilient — able to recover after difficulty; Ritual — a prescribed ceremony or repeatedly followed routine; Burden — a load or difficult responsibility; Adapt — change to suit conditions; Thrive — grow or develop successfully.

items.positive: POSITIVE: Jubilant, Tranquil, Uplifting, Serene, Hopeful, Joyful, Whimsical, Light-hearted, Celebratory, Enchanting, Comforting.
items.neutral: NEUTRAL: Reflective, Meditative, Ambiguous, Mysterious, Solemn, Thoughtful, Nostalgic, Clinical, Detached, Philosophical, Measured, Serious.
items.negative: NEGATIVE: Oppressive, Melancholic, Foreboding, Bleak, Dismal, Hostile, Anxious, Isolated, Harrowing, Desolate.

items.supportive: SUPPORTIVE: Admiring, Affirming, Endorsing, Celebratory, Sympathetic, Encouraging, Empathetic, Respectful, Optimistic.
items.critical: CRITICAL: Condemning, Dismissive, Disparaging, Disapproving, Concerned, Sceptical, Alarmed, Cautionary, Cynical, Mocking, Critical.
items.balanced: BALANCED: Neutral, Objective, Measured, Analytical, Tentative, Contemplative, Evaluative, Inquisitive, Informative, Reserved, Considered.

synthesis.title: Synthesis sentence starters
items: Both texts show that…
While one writer believes…, the other…
A shared idea in both extracts is…
Text A highlights ____, whereas Text B emphasises ____.
Together, the texts suggest that…

shadesOfMeaning.title: Shades of meaning — choose your word carefully
items: Barren: unproductive or lacking vegetation; desolate: deserted, bleak, or feeling very lonely. The meanings can overlap in a landscape.
Endure: experience or persist through difficulty; tolerate: allow or put up with something unwelcome. Tolerate can concern serious harm, not only mild annoyance.
Relentless: continuing without easing; determined: firmly resolved to achieve a goal. Either can be positive or negative in context.

spag.title: SPaG essentials
items: It’s = it is / it has; its = belonging to it. Possessive yours, hers, ours and theirs also have no apostrophe.
A fused sentence or comma splice joins independent clauses incorrectly. Use a full stop, a suitable semicolon, or a conjunction with appropriate punctuation.
Their is possessive; there can indicate place or existence; they’re = they are.
Your is possessive; you’re = you are.
In standard writing use should have or should’ve, not should of. The same applies to could have and might have.
Possessive nouns: the student’s book (one student); the students’ books (more than one student).

spelling.title: British vs American spelling
items: −our / −or: colour/color, honour/honor, behaviour/behavior, favour/favor, neighbour/neighbor.
−re / −er: centre/center, theatre/theater, metre/meter, litre/liter, calibre/caliber.
Many British words allow -ise or -ize (organise/organize); American spelling usually uses -ize. Analyse/analyze is a separate -yse/-yze pattern.
Double consonants: travelling/traveling, labelled/labeled, cancelled/canceled, marvellous/marvelous.
Misc: aeroplane/airplane, maths/math, programme/program, grey/gray, cheque/check.
Use a consistent recognised spelling variety and follow any explicit teacher or task instruction; British spelling is not a universal requirement of English analysis.

devicesExamples.title: Literary devices with worked examples
items: Personification — 'The wind whispered through the trees.'
Zoomorphism — describing humans as animals: 'She fought like a tiger.'
Repetition — emphasises emotion: 'I will not, I will not, I will not give up.'
Metaphor — 'Time is a thief.'
Alliteration — 'wild and windy weather.'
Hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration: 'I've told you a million times.'
Sensory imagery — appeals to five senses.
Simile — comparison with like/as: 'as cold as ice.'

extras.title: English — Extras
extras.intro: Topics that go deeper than the G9 revision list — critical thinking, classic literature, advanced vocabulary, exam-ready quotes.

criticalThinking.title: Critical thinking
items: Identify the claim and its scope: what exactly is being asserted?
Check whether the evidence is relevant, reliable and sufficient; distinguish evidence from an illustrative anecdote.
A straw man distorts an opponent’s position; a false dichotomy excludes plausible options; an ad hominem attacks the person instead of addressing the argument.
Expert testimony can be relevant evidence. An appeal to authority is weak when the expertise is irrelevant or substitutes for support.
Evaluate authorship, methods, evidence, purpose and corroboration. Publication format alone does not create a fixed reliability ranking.

shakespeare.title: Shakespeare — quick intro
shakespeare.body: Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote plays and sonnets. Macbeth and Hamlet are tragedies; A Midsummer Night’s Dream is a comedy. Iambic pentameter is a metrical pattern of five iambic feet (typically unstressed then stressed), often giving ten syllables; actual lines can vary. Identify the pattern and meaningful departures, rather than counting syllables alone.

vocab.title: Advanced vocabulary for essays
items: Ubiquitous — present or found everywhere or in many places; stronger than merely common.
Profound — very deep, intense or insightful, depending on context.
Articulate (verb) — express clearly; articulate (adjective) — able to express ideas clearly.
Paradox — a statement or situation that seems contradictory; resolving it may reveal an insight, but not every paradox states a truth.
Catalyst — figuratively, someone or something that brings about or speeds change; the chemistry meaning is more specific.
Pivotal — central to how something develops or succeeds.
Inevitable — unable to be avoided; use only when that strong claim is justified.
Furthermore / moreover — introduce an additional supporting point.
Notwithstanding — despite, or nevertheless; a formal expression whose position affects its grammar.
Consequently / therefore — introduce a result or inference; the logical connection still needs support.

essayQuotes.title: Using quotations responsibly
items: Use a quotation only when its exact wording and attribution can be checked in a primary text.
Give the speaker and work when relevant: a fictional character’s words are not automatically the author’s own view.
Analyse how the quotation supports your argument. A famous saying does not prove a factual claim.

poetry.title: Analysing poetry
poetry.body: Read for speaker, situation and development. Form includes lines, stanzas and their organisation. Rhyme scheme maps end rhymes; metre describes patterns of stressed and unstressed syllables. Imagery evokes sensory experience; tone is the speaker’s or text’s attitude, while mood is the atmosphere a reader may experience. Theme is an explored idea, not just a one-word topic. Support interpretations with precise wording and allow for shifts and ambiguity.

textTypesPage.title: Text Types (Criterion C)
textTypesPage.intro: You may be asked to write one of these text types for Criterion C. Each has its own format and conventions, so check them before you start writing.

essay.name: Essay
essay.rule: An essay is a short prose text in free composition: the writer gives a personal view on a topic, and an argument or a final conclusion is optional. An argumentative essay states a thesis and proves it paragraph by paragraph; the five-paragraph plan of a timed exam answer is a separate school scheme. The task sets the purpose, register, length and whether the first person is allowed.
examples: Thesis: 'Libraries should stay open late, because not every student has a quiet place to study at home.'
Supporting evidence: 'Mara finishes her history essays in the library because it is quieter than home. A library open late would help every student in the same position.'
Formal: 'This essay argues that libraries should stay open late.' Personal: 'I used to think libraries were only for exams.' Use the first person only when the task allows it.
essay.tip: In an argumentative essay, answer the question and state your thesis in the introduction, then prove it: argue, don't list.

letter.name: Letter
letter.rule: A letter is a written message to a specific recipient. It needs a greeting that suits your relationship with the reader, a clear body and a closing. Layout conventions for formal letters can differ between countries and organisations.
examples: Formal opening: 'Dear Ms Taylor,' with the closing 'Yours sincerely, Sam'. If you do not know the addressee's name, open with 'Dear Sir/Madam' and close with 'Yours faithfully'.
Informal opening: 'Dear Granny,' / closing: 'Love, Sam' or 'Best wishes,'.

Letter of complaint: 'The lunch queue has taken over 20 minutes since Monday. I timed it on three days, and it reached 25 minutes on Thursday. Please open a second serving point by Friday.' The issue, the evidence, the action and the deadline come in that order.

Letter to the editor: 'The new timetable leaves our stop without a bus after 7pm. Late shift workers have no safe way home. The council should review it this month.' Short, with one clear opinion and a call to action.
letter.watchOut: DON'T mix formal and informal: never write 'Dear Sir/Madam' then 'Take care!' — register must match throughout.

email.name: Email
email.rule: An email is an electronic message with a recipient and usually a subject, greeting, body and sign-off. Its register may be formal or informal: purpose and relationship matter more than the medium.
examples: Subject: 'Request: extension on history essay deadline'
Body: 'Hi Ms Taylor, I'm writing to ask for a two-day extension on the history essay due Friday. I've been unwell since Monday. Thank you for considering this. Best wishes, Sam.'
Reply: 'Hi Sam, Thanks for letting me know. The new deadline is Sunday at 6pm. Best, Ms Taylor.'
email.tip: Put your purpose in the first sentence, because readers scan emails and the subject line decides whether they open them.

speech.name: Speech
speech.rule: A speech is prepared for listeners. State your purpose, organise ideas in a sequence listeners can follow by ear, and close clearly. Direct address, repetition or a call to action suit a persuasive speech but are not required in every speech.
examples: Hook: 'Imagine waking up tomorrow with no internet. How long before you'd cope?'
Tricolon (three parallel items): 'We need education, opportunity, and hope.'
Direct address: 'Friends, fellow students, you have the power to change this.'
Anaphora: 'We want a library that opens late. We want a garden that everyone can use. We want a school that listens.'
Call to action: 'So sign the petition. Speak to your MP. Start a group at school this week.'
speech.tip: Read your speech aloud as you write it, keep sentences short enough to say in one breath, and use dashes or ellipses to mark pauses.

newspaper.name: Newspaper Article
newspaper.rule: A newspaper article may report news, explain a topic or offer commentary. A straight news report often has a headline, byline and a lead giving key facts, followed by supporting detail; features and opinion pieces may use different structures.
examples: Headline: 'Local pupils open a community garden'
Lead: 'Pupils opened a garden beside the library on Saturday to provide a shared growing space.'
Attribution: 'Léa, who runs the garden club, said the group would meet every Saturday.' Before publishing, check every name, date, quotation and number.
newspaper.tip: In an inverted pyramid, put the most important facts first, so the story still makes sense if the editor cuts the last paragraph.

online.name: Online Article
online.rule: An online article is a piece of writing published on a website. It has no single fixed genre: a review, a guide or a personal opinion can all be published online. Tone, length and evidence depend on the audience and purpose.
examples: A subheading can state the question the section answers, for example 'Why do readers skim online?'
Links let readers inspect the evidence behind a factual claim.
A news report and a personal how-to post can both appear online, but they use different registers.
online.tip: Give readers a clear route through the information: numerical limits on paragraph length or subheading frequency are design choices, not genre rules.

blog.name: Blog Article
blog.rule: A blog post is an entry in a regularly updated online journal. Its entries are arranged by date. It may be personal, professional, explanatory or persuasive. First person and conversational language are options, not requirements.
examples: Title: 'Why I quit Netflix for a month (and what I learned)'
Opening: 'So three weeks ago, I deleted Netflix from my phone. I know — radical, right?'
Body: 'Here's the thing nobody told me about screen-time addiction...'
Closing: 'What's the one app you couldn't live without? Drop a comment below.'
Byline: 'Posted by Alex on 14 October 2026 · 4 min read'
blog.tip: Even a recognisable voice needs accurate wording and proofreading, and the level of informality should suit the intended audience.

guide.name: Revision Guide
guide.rule: A revision guide organises knowledge so that it is easy to recall. It defines terms accurately, shows worked examples and includes questions that check understanding.
examples: Heading: 'Command terms'
Definition box: 'Describe means give a clear account of what something is or looks like; explain means give reasons.'
Worked example: 'Question: Explain how the writer creates tension. Answer: the short sentences force a pause, so the reader feels the same hesitation as the character.'
Tip box: 'Always check that your answer responds to the command term in the question.'
Checklist: can you define each term without notes, and solve one example on your own?
guide.tip: Layout matters as much as content: a guide with white space and a clear hierarchy of headings is more useful than a wall of text.

script.name: Script
script.rule: A script sets out dialogue and stage directions for performance or production. Stage plays, films and radio programmes use different conventions; character names and clear descriptions of action and sound help the performers.
examples: Scene heading: 'INT. SCHOOL CAFETERIA — DAY'
Action: 'ALEX sits alone, picking at his food. SAM enters and sees him.'
Dialogue, typed as plain text: 'SAM: Mind if I sit?'
Parenthetical: '(quietly) Yeah... whatever.'
Plays and screenplays are laid out differently. In a screenplay, character names are centred above the dialogue (the Hollywood format); in a play, they usually sit at the left margin.
script.tip: Show, don't tell: write 'Alex stares at the tray without eating' rather than 'Alex is sad', and let dialogue sound like real speech rather than perfect sentences.

narrative.name: Narrative
narrative.rule: A narrative tells a connected story: characters, a setting and a conflict that changes the situation, with events in a clear time order, usually in the past tense. A narrator tells it from one point of view: 'I' (inside the story) or 'he', 'she' or 'they' (outside it).
examples: I didn't want to go to the party, but Mum had already told everyone I would be there.
Mara wanted the lead role in the summer play more than anything, but the director had already given it to her best friend.
Léa missed the last bus, so she walked home through the empty market, and that was when she heard the piano.
In the end, Sam gave the wallet back to its owner, and for the first time all week he felt lighter.
narrative.watchOut: DON'T confuse the two: a narrative is one connected story with a plot, while a diary is a set of dated entries about the writer's own life, and a single entry does not need a plot.

diary.name: Diary
diary.rule: A diary is a set of dated entries in which the writer records personal experience, thoughts and feelings. Entries are written in the first person, in an informal register, mainly for the writer alone. Each entry usually covers one day or a short period.
examples: Monday 12 October. I passed the maths test, and I still can't quite believe it.
I shouldn't have shouted at Alex this morning. I was tired, but that's no excuse, so I'll apologise tomorrow.
Honestly, another late train. I missed the start of the film, and my hands are freezing.
Saturday 10 October. Went to the market with Sam, bought too many peaches and no batteries.
diary.watchOut: DON'T polish a diary entry like a finished essay: fragments and unfinished thoughts are normal, and a neat final paragraph is not needed.

devicesPage.title: Literary Devices
devicesPage.intro: Identify devices when reading; use them deliberately when writing.

metaphor.name: Metaphor
metaphor.rule: A metaphor describes one thing in terms of another, transferring features or associations without presenting a literal identity. It can be a noun, verb or longer image; it need not say “X is Y”.
examples: “Her argument collapsed.” An argument is presented as a structure that can fall.
“The classroom was a zoo before the test.” The noise and disorder of the room are described as the chaos of a zoo.
metaphor.tip: Name both things the metaphor links and the feature that is transferred between them.

simile.name: Simile
simile.rule: A simile compares two unlike things directly, using the words “like” or “as”, to show a shared quality. Its effect depends on the particular comparison and context; it is not inherently weaker than a metaphor.
examples: “Her voice was like sandpaper.” The comparison suggests a rough sound.
“He waited as still as a statue.” The comparison highlights lack of movement.
“I like music” expresses a preference and is not a simile.
simile.tip: Quote the whole comparison, not just the noun, and explain why the writer chose this pairing.

anaphora.name: Anaphora
anaphora.rule: Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses, sentences or verse lines. This repeated opening can connect ideas and build emphasis.
examples: “We need time. We need trust. We need change.” Each sentence begins “We need”.
“Nobody came. Nobody called. Nobody cared.” Each sentence begins with “Nobody”.
anaphora.tip: Two repetitions may be a coincidence; three or more form a pattern worth commenting on.

alliteration.name: Alliteration
alliteration.rule: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds, especially at the beginnings of nearby stressed words or syllables. It is a sound pattern, not simply repeated spelling.
examples: “Wild and windy weather” repeats /w/.
“City” and “cat” start with the same letter but different sounds, /s/ and /k/.
“Silent streets” repeats /s/ and also illustrates sibilance, a repeated hissing sound.
alliteration.tip: A sound does not carry a fixed emotion by itself: support claims such as “menacing” or “gentle” with the words and situation.

personification.name: Personification
personification.rule: Personification presents an object, animal, natural force or abstract idea as a person, giving it human qualities, intentions or behaviour. It often works through metaphor.
examples: “The clock scolded me for being late.” Scolding gives the clock a human social role.
“Hope refused to leave.” An abstract idea is given human determination.
“The dog ran” is literal animal behaviour, so it is not personification.
personification.tip: A human-like action such as swallowing can be done by animals too, so it does not automatically personify. Explain the image first, then choose the label.

hyperbole.name: Hyperbole
hyperbole.rule: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration intended to emphasise a feeling or point, rather than to be accepted as a literal measurement or fact.
examples: “I have waited a thousand years!” exaggerates a long or frustrating wait.
“This bag weighs a ton” exaggerates how heavy the bag is, so carrying it may feel like a huge effort.
hyperbole.tip: Say what is exaggerated and what effect the exaggeration has on the reader.

rhetoricalQuestion.name: Rhetorical question
rhetoricalQuestion.rule: A rhetorical question is asked mainly to make a point, provoke thought or express a feeling, rather than to obtain new information from an answer.
examples: “Who would choose more homework?” in a speech against extra tasks expects the answer “nobody”.
“How long can we ignore this?” challenges the audience to act.
rhetoricalQuestion.tip: Decide first whether the writer expects an answer, then explain the effect.

imagery.name: Imagery
imagery.rule: Imagery is language that evokes sensory experience: sight, sound, smell, taste or touch. It may be literal description or figurative language.
examples: “The damp wool scratched her neck.” Touch is central.
“A sharp lemon scent filled the room.” Smell is central.
imagery.tip: Name the sense the description appeals to and the mood it creates.

onomatopoeia.name: Onomatopoeia
onomatopoeia.rule: Onomatopoeia uses a word whose sound imitates or suggests the sound it names. These imitations are conventional and vary between languages.
examples: “Buzz”, “hiss” and “clang” suggest sounds through pronunciation.
A dog’s bark is “woof” in English but “gav” in Russian, so each language has its own imitation.
onomatopoeia.tip: Say which sound the word imitates and how that sound supports the meaning.

irony.name: Irony
irony.rule: Irony involves a meaningful gap between words and intended meaning, expectation and outcome, or the knowledge of characters and audience. Common categories are verbal, situational and dramatic irony.
examples: Verbal: “Perfect timing!” after a badly timed interruption.
Situational: a campaign for silence is disrupted by its own loudspeaker.
Dramatic: the audience knows a guest is plotting against an unsuspecting host.
irony.tip: Name the type of irony first, then explain the gap that creates it.

symbolism.name: Symbolism
symbolism.rule: Symbolism uses something concrete, such as an object, image or action, to suggest meaning beyond its literal role. A symbol’s meaning is established by the work and its cultural context.
examples: A character who keeps washing her hands may suggest guilt, not just cleanliness.
A locked gate might suggest exclusion if the surrounding text supports that reading.
symbolism.tip: Check where the image recurs before you call it a symbol: a recurring element is a motif and becomes a symbol only when it carries further meaning.

foreshadowing.name: Foreshadowing
foreshadowing.rule: Foreshadowing is an earlier detail that hints at a later development. The connection may create anticipation on a first reading or become clear only after the event.
examples: A story mentions a bridge’s damaged support before that bridge later collapses.
Early in the story, a character leaves the back door unlocked “for a minute”. Later, that door is how the intruder gets in.
foreshadowing.tip: Name the later event the detail points to, then explain the link.

grammarPage.title: Grammar Essentials
grammarPage.intro: Frequent grammar pitfalls and the rules that fix them.

present.name: Present simple
present.use: Present simple expresses habits, general states and facts; it can also refer to scheduled future events. Tense is a grammatical form, whereas time is when an event occurs.
present.form: Most verbs: I/you/we/they + base form; he/she/it + -s/-es. Questions and negatives use do/does + base form. Be is different: am/is/are; is she…?; she is not….
examples: She writes every weekend.
Water boils at 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.
The train leaves at seven tomorrow.
He does not eat meat.
present.tip: Don't forget the −s on third person singular: 'He goes' (not 'He go'). For verbs ending in −y after consonant: study → studies.

presentCont.name: Present continuous (progressive)
presentCont.use: Present continuous combines present-tense be with the progressive aspect: a situation is viewed as in progress around now, temporary, changing or arranged for the future.
presentCont.form: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing. Negative: am/is/are + not + verb-ing. Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + verb-ing?
examples: She is writing an essay (right now).
I'm staying with my aunt this week (temporary).
We're meeting Tom at 6 (future arrangement).
presentCont.watchOut: Stative meanings usually take simple forms: I know. Some verbs have dynamic uses: I am seeing the dentist tomorrow; I am thinking about your idea.

past.name: Past simple
past.use: Past simple presents events or states in a finished past period. The time can be stated or understood from context; it need not appear as an exact date.
past.form: Regular verbs usually take -ed; irregular verbs have learned forms such as went. Questions/negatives normally use did + base form. Be uses was/were: Was she ready? She was not ready.
examples: She wrote three essays yesterday.
We went to Paris last summer.
He didn't see the film.
Did you eat lunch?
past.tip: Time markers: yesterday, last (week / year), ago, in 2020, when I was younger.

pastCont.name: Past continuous
pastCont.use: The past continuous presents an event as already in progress at a past reference time: was/were + verb-ing. It often supplies background to another event; that event need not interrupt or stop it.
examples: She was writing when the lights went out.
While we were having dinner, the phone rang.
It was raining all morning.
pastCont.tip: The progressive presents an action from within its duration; simple past presents the event as a whole. This is a difference in viewpoint, not a rule that one action must be long and the other short.

presentPerfect.name: Present perfect
presentPerfect.use: Present perfect relates a situation before now to the present: experience so far, a current result, or a state continuing until now. It is present tense with perfect aspect, not a direct equivalent of Russian perfective aspect.
presentPerfect.form: Subject + have/has + past participle. Negative: have/has + not + pp. Question: Have/Has + subject + pp?
examples: She has written three essays (this year — still ongoing).
I've never been to Japan (life experience).
We've lived here since 2010 (started past, continues).
He's just finished his homework (recent).
presentPerfect.watchOut: In standard British usage, a finished-time expression such as yesterday normally takes past simple. For, since, already and just are clues to meaning, not automatic selectors of a tense.

future.name: Future reference: will, be going to, present continuous
future.use: English refers to future time through several constructions. Will often expresses predictions, offers or decisions; be going to often signals an intention or current evidence; present continuous often signals an arrangement. Their meanings can overlap.
future.form: Will: subject + will + base verb. Going to: subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb.
examples: 'I'll help you with that.' (just decided).
'It will rain tomorrow.' (prediction).
'I'm going to study medicine.' (plan).
'Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.' (evidence-based).
'I'm meeting Alex at 4.' (arrangement).
future.tip: In a grammatical account based on verb inflection, English has present and past tenses; “future tense” is a common classroom label for future constructions. Choose the form for meaning, not merely to create variety.

comma.name: Comma (,)
comma.use: Commas mark grammatical boundaries: list items, introductory elements and non-essential information. They can separate independent clauses when joined by a coordinating conjunction; a spoken pause alone is not a rule.
examples: I bought bread, cheese, and milk. (list)
After the storm, the village was flooded. (introductory phrase)
Macbeth, who was once loyal, becomes a tyrant. (non-defining clause)
The film was long, but I enjoyed it. (before coordinating conjunction)
comma.watchOut: Don't use a comma to join two complete sentences (this is a 'comma splice'): WRONG — 'I went out, it was cold.' Use a full stop, semicolon, or conjunction.

semicolon.name: Semicolon (;)
semicolon.use: A semicolon can link closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. It can also separate list items that already contain commas; those items need not be complete clauses.
examples: Macbeth kills Duncan; immediately he is haunted by guilt.
She didn't speak; she just walked away.
We visited Cairo, Egypt; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.
semicolon.tip: For the clause-linking use, both sides must be independent clauses and their ideas must be closely related. In a complex list, the items need not be complete clauses.

colon.name: Colon (:)
colon.use: A colon directs the reader to an explanation, example, list or quotation that follows. In ordinary prose, an introductory clause is normally complete: “We need two things: time and patience.”
examples: She had three goals: ambition, power, and survival.
Macbeth makes one fatal mistake: he listens to the witches.
Lady Macbeth declares: 'Unsex me here.'
colon.watchOut: For the list/explanation use in ordinary prose, the introduction is normally a complete clause. Do not separate a verb or preposition from its complement: write “We bought bread and milk”, not “We bought: bread and milk”.

apostrophe.name: Apostrophe (')
apostrophe.use: An apostrophe marks omitted letters in contractions, such as don’t, or forms many genitives, such as the teacher’s advice. A genitive expresses a relationship, not always literal ownership. Ordinary noun plurals do not take an apostrophe.
examples: Sam's book — book belongs to Sam (singular owner).
The students' essays — essays of the students (plural owners).
Don't = do not. It's = it is. They're = they are.
James's coat / James' coat — both accepted; pick one and be consistent.
apostrophe.watchOut: Possessive its, yours, hers, ours and theirs have no apostrophe. This does not apply to every pronoun: one’s and someone’s do take one. It’s can mean it is or it has.

dash.name: Dash (—)
dash.use: An em dash can set off an interruption, an aside or an emphatic addition. Its effect depends on the sentence and the publication’s style; it is not automatically dramatic.
examples: Macbeth — once loyal, now a tyrant — falls in the final battle.
She wanted only one thing — power.
He paused — then drew the dagger.
dash.tip: An em dash (—) and a hyphen (-) have different jobs. Spaces around a dash vary by style guide. Use punctuation to make the sentence structure clear.

agreement.title: Subject–verb agreement
agreement.body: Subject–verb agreement means choosing a finite verb form that fits the subject’s person and number where English marks those distinctions: I am, she is, they are; he works, they work. An intervening noun does not usually control the verb, and collective nouns allow variation by meaning and variety of English.
rules: Singular: The boy runs. Plural: The boys run. Be also distinguishes I am, she is and they are.
Find the head of the subject: The list of items is on the table. Here list governs agreement.
With mixed-number either/or or neither/nor subjects, agreement with the nearer subject is common. Reword an awkward sentence if needed.
In British English, collective nouns may take singular or plural agreement depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as members. American usage more often favours singular agreement.
Each, everyone, nobody and somebody normally take a singular verb. Every is normally a determiner: every student has a book.
A number of students are absent; the number of students is rising.

yourYoure.name: your vs you're
yourYoure.rule: Your is a possessive determiner used before a noun phrase: your book, your new idea. You’re contracts you are and supplies a subject plus verb: you’re ready. To express possession without a following noun, use yours.
examples: Is this your book? (possessive)
You're late again. (you are)
yourYoure.tip: Try expanding you’re to you are. Use your when a following noun belongs or relates to the person addressed.

itsIts.name: its vs it's
itsIts.rule: Its is a possessive determiner for something referred to as it: its colour, its main purpose. It’s is the contraction of it is or it has: it’s cold; it’s changed. Possessive its has no apostrophe.
examples: The dog wagged its tail. (possessive)
It's raining. (it is)
It's been a long day. (it has)
itsIts.tip: Expand it’s to it is or it has. Possessive its has no apostrophe: the bird spread its wings.

thereTheirTheyre.name: there / their / they're
thereTheirTheyre.rule: There can point to a place or introduce existence, as in there is a problem. Their is a possessive determiner before a noun phrase, corresponding to they, including singular they: their work. They’re contracts they are. These words sound alike but have different grammatical jobs.
examples: Put it over there. (place)
There are five students. (there are)
Their essays were excellent. (belonging to them)
They're studying for the exam. (they are)
thereTheirTheyre.tip: There can indicate a place or introduce existence; their is possessive; they’re expands to they are. Decide by meaning and sentence structure.

lessFewer.name: less vs fewer
lessFewer.rule: In formal edited English, fewer normally modifies plural count nouns; less normally modifies uncountable nouns. Less is also usual with amounts viewed as a single quantity, such as less than ten minutes.
examples: Fewer cars on the road this morning.
We have less time than we thought.
I made fewer mistakes than last week.
lessFewer.tip: Time meaning duration is uncountable: less time. Times meaning occasions is countable: fewer times. Informal usage varies.

affectEffect.name: affect vs effect
affectEffect.rule: Affect is commonly a verb meaning influence; effect is commonly a noun meaning result. These are the most frequent uses, not the only word classes.
examples: The decision will affect everyone. (verb)
The effect of the decision was huge. (noun)
Climate change affects ecosystems. (verb)
One effect of climate change is sea level rise. (noun)
affectEffect.tip: Effect can be a verb meaning bring about: effect change. Affect can be a technical noun for an observable emotional state or expression. Check the intended meaning.

thanThen.name: than vs then
thanThen.rule: Than introduces a comparison. Then commonly refers to a time, the next step, or a consequence in an if…then relationship.
examples: She is taller than her brother. (comparison)
First we ate, then we walked home. (sequence)
If it rains, then we'll stay in. (consequence)
thanThen.tip: Comparison → think 'compare', both have an A. Time → then has 'en' like 'when'.

readingPage.title: Reading Skills
readingPage.intro: How to break down unseen texts in exam conditions.

skim.name: Skim
skim.use: Read quickly for the overall subject, purpose and organisation before examining details.
skim.rule: Look at the title, the headings, the opening and closing lines, and any sentence that stands out. Adjust the method to the text: a poem or a dialogue may not state its main idea at the start or the end.
skim.tip: Do not stop at unfamiliar words. Read on, then go back only if the word blocks the main idea.

scan.name: Scan
scan.use: Use it when you need one specific piece of information, such as a name, a date, a keyword or a quotation.
scan.rule: Choose the detail you need, then search for distinctive names, numbers or related words. Once you find a candidate, read the surrounding sentences carefully to check its meaning.
examples: A question asks when the storm arrived. Scan for “storm” and any dates or times, then check that the date appears in the sentence about the storm.
Scanning rarely finds a metaphor, because there is usually no single keyword to search for. You have to read for meaning instead.

annotate.name: Annotate
annotate.use: Mark up the text as you read so you can find evidence quickly when answering.
annotate.rule: Add brief notes that help you understand and revisit the text: mark a relevant phrase, propose its effect, and record any question or possible shift in tone.
annotate.tip: Use the same few marks every time, for example a box around a device and a wavy line for tone, so that each mark means the same thing throughout the text. Colouring every line makes key evidence harder to find.

infer.name: Infer
infer.use: Read between the lines — what is the author IMPLYING but not directly saying?
infer.rule: An inference is a conclusion supported by textual clues and relevant background knowledge. Separate what the text states from what you infer and consider other plausible explanations.
examples: “She slammed the door” suggests anger. If the previous lines describe a sudden draught, the reader should infer a physical cause instead.
“The garden had gone grey and silent” suggests the setting mirrors someone’s grief. The garden cannot literally grieve, so the reader must work out the link.

literal.name: Literal questions
literal.use: Ask for information stated explicitly in the text.
literal.rule: Locate the relevant statement and quote it accurately or paraphrase it. Follow the question’s wording and use the mark allocation to decide how many details to give.
examples: “State one reason Sam is late.” Quote the line that gives the reason directly, for example “The bus broke down on the way.”
“Name two effects of climate change mentioned in the text.” Give two effects the text states. An effect from your own knowledge does not answer this question, however accurate it is.

inferential.name: Inferential questions
inferential.use: An inferential question asks for a conclusion supported by the text but not directly stated in it, such as a possible motive or attitude.
inferential.rule: Identify a specific clue, explain the reasoning from that clue to your conclusion, and check it against the surrounding text. Distinguish a well-supported inference from a possible reading or an unsupported guess.
examples: If a relationship is described as “cold”, emotional detachment is a possible inference. The word may also mean a physical temperature, so decide which meaning the context supports.

language.name: Language analysis
language.use: Asks how the writer creates meaning: 'How does the writer use language?'
language.rule: Select precise wording, explain its meaning and associations, and connect these to a supported interpretation. Name a technique when the label helps explain the choice.
examples: In the phrase “a sea of doubt”, doubt is imagined as a vast surrounding mass; this may suggest being overwhelmed.
language.tip: Never say 'the writer uses a metaphor to make it more interesting.' Always say WHAT specific feeling, image, or idea the technique creates.

evaluation.name: Evaluation questions
evaluation.use: An evaluation question asks for a critical judgement, for example “How effective is X?” or “To what extent…?”
evaluation.rule: Make a judgement about the feature named in the question. Support it with relevant details and explain how they bear on your judgement. Discuss limits or counter-evidence where they matter; follow the task’s actual requirements.
examples: For a question about imagery, identify an image, explain its effect in context and judge how it serves the text’s purpose. A different supported interpretation may also be valid.

PEEL.title: PEEL paragraph structure
PEEL.body: PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explain, Link) is a planning scaffold for an analytical paragraph. It helps connect a claim, evidence and reasoning; it is not an exam rule or a guaranteed marking checklist.

steps.p: POINT — open with your topic sentence: the specific claim this paragraph will prove. For example, “The writer presents Sam as more anxious than his brother at the start of the story.”
steps.e1: EVIDENCE — use a relevant short quotation or precise reference. For example, “Sam checked the lock three times while his brother was already asleep.”
steps.e2: EXPLAIN — show how the wording supports your claim. “Three times” suggests that one check is never enough for Sam, and the contrast with his sleeping brother shows that his anxiety is greater. Relate this reading to the rest of the paragraph.
steps.l: LINK — connect back to the question and forward to the next paragraph. For example, “This anxiety contrasts sharply with his brother’s calm, setting up the tension the next paragraph explores.”

PEEL.tip: Adapt the amount of evidence to your argument. A paragraph may need several pieces of evidence, each with its own explanation; follow the task and its assessment criteria.

essaysPage.title: Essay Practice
essaysPage.intro: Sample essay prompts in the IB MYP style. Plan with a thesis, three points, and a conclusion.

essayPrompts.prompt: 'Social media does more harm than good.' Discuss.
essayPrompts.tips: Balance both sides. State your position clearly. Use real examples (Instagram, TikTok). Conclude decisively.

essayPrompts.prompt: 'School uniforms should be abolished.' Argue for or against.
essayPrompts.tips: Take one side firmly. Three reasons with evidence. Address counterargument and refute it.

essayPrompts.prompt: Write a story beginning with: 'The lights flickered, and then…'
essayPrompts.tips: Establish setting. Use varied sentence structure. Include sensory detail. End with a twist or resonance.

essayPrompts.prompt: Describe a place that is special to you. Bring it to life through the five senses.
essayPrompts.tips: Sight, sound, smell, touch, taste. Avoid clichés. Use figurative language sparingly.

essayPrompts.prompt: Write a speech persuading your school to take action on climate change.
essayPrompts.tips: Direct address ('We must…'). Rhetorical question. Tripartite list. Call to action at the end.

checklist: Match the requested purpose, audience, form and register.
Organise connected ideas into clear paragraphs.
Choose sentence structures that serve the meaning.
Use literary devices when they help the intended effect; there is no required quota.
Select precise details and balance showing with useful explanation.
Proofread spelling, punctuation and the meaning of tense changes.
